ROME, Oct 14 : Chinese automakers looking to expand production capacity in Europe have ruled out Italy because of a lack of suitable factories, Italian industry minister Adolfo Urso said on Wednesday.  Chinese producers are looking to establish manufacturing plants inside the European Union as Brussels works on rules that will set minimum local content limits for electric vehicles sold in the bloc.  "They are touring Europe and what are they asking for? A turnkey factory," Urso told lawmakers in Rome, referring to a production site that would be ready to operate immediately. He said Chinese auto industry representatives, including BYD's European adviser Alfredo Altavilla, had visited plants in Italy and met Urso several times without finding suitable locations.

This was because Stellantis, Italy's sole major auto producer, has decided to produce cars in partnership with Chinese companies rather than give up any of its Italian factories, Urso said. "Stellantis, unlike other industry players, has not closed any plants in Italy and therefore has no turnkey facilities available to hand over to Chinese automakers," the minister said during a parliamentary questions session.  Altavilla told Reuters last month that BYD, unlike some of its Chinese competitors, aimed to buy and fully own a European plant rather than share it with local partners, adding that it was focusing on Spain and France.

LONDON, Oct 14 : US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday. Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence. But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values". Palantir's supply of software for the US military and immigration services, plus billionaire co-founder Peter Thiel's political views, have drawn scrutiny as European governments grow increasingly wary about dependency on US tech platforms.

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : The European Commission said on Wednesday it was "in dialogue with Google" over actions the company may take in response to the $1 billion fines imposed by the EU in July and required changes to its app store and its search engine. The Commission has fined Alphabet's Google €460 million ($511.43 million) and €430 million respectively for favouring its own services in shopping, hotels, transport and sports search results and for the restrictions for app developers on its app store Google Play. "We are currently in dialogue with Google, so I'll not prejudge the outcome of this dialogue, but I can guarantee you that the Commission services are currently in dialogue with Google precisely on this issue," spokesperson Thomas Regnier said during a daily EU press briefing. The Commission ordered Google to comply with recommendations to treat rivals in a fair and non-discriminatory manner and allow app developers to steer users away from its app store within 60 days.

MEXICO CITY, Oct 14 : Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she will sign a presidential decree later on Wednesday requiring digital platforms, including social networks and streaming sites, to shield children and teenagers from violent, sexual and other harmful content. The decree, which will step up scrutiny of big technology companies in Latin America's second largest economy, comes after an attack by two 18-year-old former students on a high school in the northern state of Coahuila in early October left one person dead and wounded three others. Digital platforms will have one month to come into compliance with the decree, government adviser Luisa Maria Alcalde said. Sheinbaum added that if the decree was not followed by firms, the government would back a bill to levy punishments against platforms.

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : Sports technology company Sportradar Group was hit with antitrust complaints to EU and UK regulators on Wednesday by sportsbook software company Altenar Technologies, which accused it of blocking rivals' access to its live official sports data. Swiss-headquartered Sportradar is a leading content provider of betting-related content in major sports including tennis, soccer and basketball. Its exclusive deals with major sports leagues MLB, NBA, ATP, and NHL include data collection and distribution rights, as well as the right to provide live betting odds derived from that data. The complaints follow an antitrust lawsuit Altenar filed in a US court in April, alleging Sportradar has monopolised the market for live official sports data in the US and stifled competition.

The European Commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "We believe Sportradar is using its control of essential sports data to shut out businesses with a competing offer," an Altenar spokesperson said. "Bookmakers across the EU and UK need a choice of suppliers and a market that supports competition and innovation. We are asking the European Commission and the CMA to intervene and ensure that independent providers can compete on fair terms," the spokesperson said. Altenar is also asking the CMA to impose interim measures restoring access to essential data and odds pending the outcome of an investigation. EU antitrust violations can result in fines of up to 10 per cent of a company's annual global turnover.

NEW YORK, Oct 14 : Japan will invest up to $21 billion in two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries, the company said on Wednesday.   Shares of the Malta, New York-based company rose more than 4 per cent in early trading. They have gained more than 33 per cent this year. The move is part of a deal for Japan to invest $550 billion in the US struck by President Donald Trump's administration last year in return for the US lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25 per cent to 15 per cent.  The US will take a stake in the new chip factories, but Japan will provide all of the investment capital, GlobalFoundries said.

The company, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Co, will earn fees from building and operating the factories, as well as licensing chip manufacturing technology to them.  In a separate agreement, the US government will take a 4 per cent stake in GlobalFoundries, bringing its total ownership of the chipmaker to about 7 per cent, GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters. Breen said GlobalFoundries would manage customer relationships, and initial customers for the New York factories include Japan's Renesas Electronics and iPhone maker Apple.   "We definitely would like to give priority to US and Japanese customers," he said. "Ultimately, I expect other companies that aren't US and Japanese will also be part of the demand, but we'll obviously go through a process after announcement to finalize the exact who gets what over what timeframe." Japan has so far announced two batches of projects worth over $100 billion combined under the investment scheme. Under the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flows from investments will be split evenly between the two countries until a specific allocation is reached, after which 90 per cent will go to the US. GlobalFoundries' Breen said that at least some of the capital investment by Japan will flow back to chip-manufacturing toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron and other Japanese firms that along with US rivals dominate the supply chain. "Obviously, we have a strong interest in the Japanese equipment suppliers to be part of it," Breen said. "We will be very open-minded, but we'll definitely engage very much with the Japanese ecosystem because they have great technologies."

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK, Oct 14 : Thailand's return to economic growth of about 3 per cent is "definitely possible" within three years if it can tackle some of its structural issues, a deputy central bank governor said on Wednesday, signalling alignment with the government's stance. The Bank of Thailand's monetary policy will remain accommodative for now and the policy rate, currently at 1.00 per cent, will normalise only when the economy is ready, Piti Disyatat, the deputy governor for monetary stability, told Reuters.  Piti said he expects the economy to grow 2.3 per cent or slightly higher this year and to expand by 1.8 per cent in 2027. The central bank's baseline scenario is to get back to a 2.8 per cent to 3 per cent range the year after.    "In the more distant future, two or three years horizon, we do think our potential trend growth is around 2.8 per cent to 3 per cent. So it is definitely possible to grow to 3 per cent and we expect growth to get to that level," he said in an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings.

"It's subject to not having negative shocks and also partly subject to some of the constraints that are within our control, the so-called more structural things that can be alleviated." Backed by a government push for new investments in key sectors such as semiconductors and data centres, Thailand's economy is expected to grow by 2.5 per cent next year and potentially by 3 per cent within the next three years, Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas told Reuters last month. In an interview last month, Don Nakornthab, Bank of Thailand assistant governor for monetary policy, said the Thai economy's potential growth rate stood at 2.7 per cent, which would take four to five years to reach. RATE CUT 'HARD TO IMAGINE' Southeast Asia's second-largest economy has struggled in recent years compared to other countries in the region, weighed down by weak demand and stubbornly high levels of household debt. The economy expanded 1.9 per cent annually in the second quarter of 2026, down sharply from 2.8 per cent in the previous quarter. The central bank left its key interest rate unchanged at 1.00 per cent in August and cut its policy rate six times between October 2024 and February, amounting to a total of 150 basis points, as it sought to give a boost to the economy. It will next review policy on October 28. "We don't foresee any reductions in rates," Piti said. "It's hard to imagine a cut unless there's a big shock hit, because 1 per cent is low historically. We've never been at 1 per cent outside of crisis times."  He added: "Definitely, I think at some point we will have to normalise interest rates when the economy is ready."

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK, Oct 14 : Japan's top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura said on Wednesday the investment activities of the country's Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) are supporting the "function and liquidity" of global financial markets. Japan had responded quite early to the challenges of a rapidly ageing population through measures such as introducing universal pensions and healthcare systems in 1961, Mimura said in a panel on demographics and ageing population held during the IMF meetings in Bangkok. Such steps created positive side effects, such as a "very healthy" workforce and a dramatic accumulation of pension funds, he said, with the GPIF now the world's biggest institutional investor. "In this way, the proactive and early introduction of policies not only supported us in responding, or better responding, to population ageing, but also gave us a lot of positive by-products," said Mimura, who is Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs. GPIF reported a record quarterly investment gain in the April-June quarter, heightening attention on whether the world's largest pension fund should rethink its investment strategy. Any shift in its portfolio strategy would reverberate across global financial markets, analysts say.

DUBLIN, Oct 14 : Recent hacking incidents perpetrated by AI agents are "early warning shots", and the world could soon face major incidents if systems are not made more secure, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis said on Wednesday. Rogue behaviour by AI agents, including corporate network hacks and, most recently, Anthropic's disclosure that an AI model submitted a false homicide tip to police, has prompted warnings from researchers and fueled concerns over the fast-advancing technology. Hassabis said there was "a lot of work to do" to adopt the kind of best practices that other fields such as biology or the nuclear sector use to secure critical systems and that some sort of international standards body would eventually be needed. "I think these (hacking incidents) are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major," Hassabis, who is also chief scientist at Google parent Alphabet, told an AI summit in Dublin.

Microsoft President Brad Smith told the conference that rogue AI behaviour had made 2026 a "sobering year" and that new AI safety laws and rules were urgently needed for safety to catch up with innovation. "No company or technology should be above the law. But we need law, we need regulation. It needs to be sensible, it needs to be balanced, it needs to take into account innovations," he said. "This allergy that some in the industry have to regulation is frankly something we need to get over." Hassabis said that, while an international standards body seemed like an obvious intervention, it would need to be nuanced and nimble so as not to stifle innovation. "So what you need to do is basically build up dynamically this kind of certification process that is proportionate with the risks as we see it and can quickly change depending on where the technology goes," he said.

LONDON, Oct 14 : Britain's media regulator Ofcom said on Wednesday it remained concerned about Elon Musk-owned X's handling of illegal hate and terrorism-related content despite improvements in response times, while disclosing new restrictions on the Grok AI chatbot. X met targets agreed with the regulator for reviewing reports of suspect content more quickly, according to the company's first quarterly performance report submitted to Ofcom. FOCUS ON COMPLIANCE AND REPORTING SYSTEMS Separately, Ofcom also said its investigation into X had moved into a new phase in which it would decide whether the platform had met its legal duties to protect people in Britain from illegal content. Ofcom opened its investigation into X in January after reports that the Grok AI chatbot was being used to create and share sexualised images that could amount to illegal content, including deepfakes involving real people and children. Ofcom said it found that some users who had not verified their age could still access pornographic content on X. Users in Britain are now blocked from viewing, generating or sharing pornographic content through Grok's image-generation tools, according to Ofcom. Companion chatbots, such as "Ani", have also been barred from engaging in sexually explicit conversations. The regulator said it would continue monitoring those changes and would keep engaging with SpaceXAI, having previously said gaps in the Online Safety Act limited its ability to investigate some activity within standalone chatbot services.

FAST

Oct 14 : Few animals show the link between size and lifespan as clearly as dogs. Within this one species, large breeds such as Great Danes typically die younger than small ones such as Chihuahuas. A new study indicates the reason may lie in how DNA changes with age in dogs. Across mammals, bigger species like elephants usually live longer lives than smaller ones like mice, but within a species that pattern can reverse. Earlier comparisons across species linked certain biological mechanisms to exceptional longevity, but those are less suited to explaining differences among individuals within a species.  "We all know that big dogs usually don't live as long as small dogs, but we have not known whether their cells actually age faster, or whether they simply hit certain diseases earlier," said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a professor at Arizona State University's School of Life Sciences and Center for Evolution and Medicine and one of the authors of the study published in the journal Science.  To find out, the researchers measured DNA methylation, chemical tags that help control which genes are switched on and off. Using age-related patterns in these tags, they built an epigenetic clock that estimated a dog's age with a median error of less than one year.

Analyzing 1,640 blood methylation profiles from 894 pet canines of various breeds, they found that larger dogs and male dogs showed signs of accelerated molecular aging, while dogs whose biological age appeared older than expected based on the profiles faced a higher risk of early death. "We found that large dogs show a faster-moving DNA methylation aging signature in blood, and that this acceleration is especially strong in parts of the genome that normally help keep 'jumping genes' quiet," Snyder-Mackler said.  Jumping genes, also called transposable elements, can copy themselves and insert into new spots in the genome. LINE1s are a type of jumping gene that is normally kept silent by DNA methylation, but their activation has been linked to genome instability, cancer and other age-related disease.  In large dogs, Snyder-Mackler said, "methylation at those regions appears to erode more quickly with age, as if the genome is losing some of the tape or clamps that keep these mobile elements suppressed."  This suggests that the shorter lives of large dogs reflect a faster molecular aging trajectory.  "If large dogs simply died earlier after following the same molecular trajectory, we would look for late-life triggers of disease or mortality. But if parts of the aging program move faster throughout adulthood, as our data suggest for the blood methylome, then there may be processes we can measure, follow over time, and potentially modify before disease appears," Snyder-Mackler said. DIFFERENCES BY SEX The researchers also found differences between male and female dogs, largely on the X chromosome — the sex chromosome that females carry in two copies and males in one. There, LINE1 elements showed higher methylation in males. Chromosomes are thread-like structures that carry genetic information inside cell nuclei. "In our genome-wide analyses, the sex signal looked distinct from the body-size signal, so I would treat that as a separate biology that needs follow-up rather than the same mechanism in disguise," Snyder-Mackler said. The trade-off between large size and longevity may be a consequence of selective breeding rather than natural evolution. Humans bred dogs to grow quickly and reach large adult sizes for tasks such as guarding, hunting and herding.  "If selection strongly favors rapid growth or large adult size before old age, late-life costs can come along for the ride," Snyder-Mackler added. Previous explanations for why large dogs tend to have shorter lives focused on growth biology. Researchers have also suggested that larger dogs may undergo more cell growth, develop more quickly or face a higher risk of cancer.  "Our study does not replace those ideas; it gives us a molecular layer downstream of body size," Snyder-Mackler said. The findings raise the possibility that slowing molecular aging could help extend healthy lifespan in larger dogs. Snyder-Mackler said, however, that lifespan is not governed by a single biological clock. Large dogs would still face breed-specific risks, meaning that slowing molecular aging would not turn a Great Dane into a Chihuahua, in terms of lifespan, but could make one component of its aging trajectory less compressed.

Source: Reuters

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : Adult content platform Stripchat, a subsidiary of Cyprus's Technius, on Thursday lost its legal challenge against EU tech regulators' decision to include it in a list of companies subject to stringent requirements under landmark online content rules after Europe's second-highest court rejected its arguments, a court statement said. Three years ago, the European Commission designated Stripchat and two other adult content companies as very large online platforms under the Digital Services Act which requires such companies to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their platforms. DSA breaches can cost companies fines as much as 6 per cent of their global turnover. Stripchat subsequently sued the Commission, which is the EU tech enforcer, at the Luxembourg-based General Court. It disagreed with how the Commission calculated its number of users, a benchmark used to assess whether a company falls under the DSA. A court statement stated that the European Commission had given Stripchat adequate reasons for its decision.

Oct 14 : The London Stock Exchange Group said on Wednesday it has partnered with Nvidia to help financial institutions process and analyse large volumes of historical market data faster and at scale using the US chipmaker's technology. LSEG, which operates the London Stock Exchange and provides data and analytics, has been expanding its offerings to support diverse demand whilst retaining licenses and control as AI also affects how businesses trade and consume data. Analysis showed that computing on Nvidia's specialised processors without creating copies of the dataset could help study every trade and price quote in seconds for insights, the company said. This would make research faster and closer to real-time as equity trading moves to 24-hour cycles, it added. "This collaboration expands how customers can draw insight from LSEG's trusted, governed Tick History. Customers want to work with detailed historical data at speed," said Ron Lefferts, co-head of data & analytics at LSEG. According to the company, its Tick History has about 110 trillion rows of data across 100 million instruments spanning 30 years and 580 exchanges, trading venues and contributors.  LSEG is the largest customer of Reuters, which provides news for its Workspace news and data platform and other products. It plans next year to launch LSE 24, a night-time trading site for some exchange-traded products.

LONDON, Oct 14 : US chipmaker Nvidia has pledged $250 million worth of computing resources to Britain over five years, to fund AI security research, bolstering the country's ambitions to become a global centre for AI governance and security. While Britain is not home to any major AI developers, it is seeking a leading role in evaluation and managing the risks posed by AI systems, partly through its AI Security Institute, one of the world's first state-backed bodies set up to assess the technology. Nvidia's founder and CEO Jensen Huang said on Wednesday that the UK would receive accelerated computing resources worth $50 million annually. They would be dedicated to agentic safety testing and help British researchers strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. "AI capability and safety must advance together," he said.

"This is how the UK turns research leadership into real-world solutions — and scientific progress into a future that benefits everyone." Scrutiny of AI safety has intensified after developers including Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed instances of rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents. Some industry figures have warned the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. British AI minister Kanishka Narayan said the donation from Nvidia would help ensure the AI of the future is "safe, secure and that serves people's best interests". Nvidia's vote of confidence in Britain comes after Microsoft President Brad Smith said in an interview on Monday that the UK was well-placed to help lead work on AI safety guidelines. The donation will connect areas of British research, including BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, which is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people as well as robotics safety at Imperial College and programmes at University College London.

Source: Reuters

BRUSSELS, Oct 14 : Google DeepMind and Alphabet's cloud service Google Cloud will provide up to 200 European scientific researchers with direct access to their frontier models, together with $3 million in compute credits, the U.S. tech giant said on Wednesday. • The move will give researchers direct access to the companies' scientific tools including AlphaFold 3, WeatherNext, AlphaGenome, AlphaEvolve, and AlphaEarth Foundations. • The companies said it will help researchers to tackle complex challenges faster, from predicting extreme weather patterns to mapping molecular structures.

Source: Reuters
